**“Beauty is truth, truth beauty.”**  
The closing couplet of the poet’s most famous ode, *Ode on a Grecian Urn*, has become an oft‑quoted aphorism and is a signature line for identifying Keats.

**“My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains”**  
These opening words launch the *Ode to a Nightingale*, one of Keats’s four major 1819 odes and a staple of Romantic poetry anthologies.

**“A thing of beauty is a joy forever.”**  
The celebrated first line of *Endymion* (1818) is repeatedly cited in literary surveys and textbooks when introducing Keats’s work.

**“La Belle Dame sans Merci”**  
The title of this haunting ballad, featuring a “fairy’s child” and “pale kings and princes,” is instantly recognizable as a Keats composition.

**“When I have fears that I may cease to be”**  
The opening phrase of a 14‑line sonnet that contemplates mortality and fame; it is one of the poet’s most frequently anthologized sonnets.

**“Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness”**  
A phrase used in the *Ode on a Grecian Urn* that describes the urn’s silent, timeless beauty; its unusual wording is a hallmark of Keats’s diction.

**“On First Looking into Chapman's Homer”**  
The title of a celebrated sonnet in which the speaker likens the experience of reading Homer to discovering a new world; it is a standard entry in Keats‑studies.

**“Bright Star, would I were steadfast as thou art”**  
The opening line of the sonnet addressed to Fanny Brawne; the poem is widely taught under the nickname “Bright Star” and is a key example of Keats’s love poetry.

**“Ode to Psyche”**  
One of the poet’s lesser‑known but frequently referenced odes, addressed to the goddess of the soul; it appears in collections of his 1819 odes.

**“Ode on Melancholy”**  
Another of the 1819 odes, recognizable by its counsel to “glut thy sorrow on a morning‑rose”; it is often paired with the Nightingale and Grecian Urn odes in curricula.

**“Hyperion”**  
The unfinished epic poem about the fall of the Titans; its title and opening line are common clues in quizzes about Keats’s mythic ambitions.

**Subject of Shelley’s elegy “Adonais”**  
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote *Adonais* to mourn the poet’s death at age 25; the elegy’s dedication is a frequent biographical clue.

**Letter describing life as a “Mansion of Many Apartments”**  
Keats’s famous correspondence with his friends uses this metaphor for the soul’s growth; the phrase appears in many biographical sketches of the poet.
